subject: Climate & Environment
title: Carbon Capture Technology
description: Learn Carbon Capture Technology in one minute.

hook.text: What if we could suck CO₂ straight out of the air and lock it underground forever?

buildup.text: Direct air capture machines use chemical filters to grab CO₂ from the atmosphere.

discovery.text: Captured carbon can be pumped into basalt rock, where it turns to stone in two years.

twist.text: It costs about $600 to capture one ton. We emit 36 billion tons per year.

climax.text: Costs are dropping fast, but capture alone cannot replace cutting emissions at the source.

punchline.text: We can vacuum the sky — but prevention beats cleanup.

quiz.question: What happens to CO₂ when pumped into basalt rock?
options: It turns to stone within two years
It escapes back into the air

details.summary: Carbon capture and storage captures CO2 from industrial sources or the atmosphere and stores it underground in geological formations. While technically proven, it remains expensive, energy-intensive, and currently operates at a tiny fraction of the scale needed to affect warming.
details.whyItMatters: CCS is essential for decarbonizing hard-to-abate industries like cement and steel. Its role in climate strategy is hotly debated between advocates and critics who see it as a fossil fuel lifeline.
takeaways: CCS captures CO2 from smokestacks or directly from the air
Current global capacity captures only about 45 million tons per year
The world emits over 36 billion tons of CO2 annually from fossil fuels

faq.question: How does direct air capture differ from point-source capture?
faq.answer: Point-source capture extracts CO2 from concentrated industrial exhaust, which is cheaper and easier. Direct air capture pulls CO2 from the ambient atmosphere where it is far more dilute, requiring much more energy and costing 5 to 10 times more per ton.

faq.question: Is carbon capture just an excuse to keep burning fossil fuels?
faq.answer: Critics argue CCS delays the transition from fossil fuels by promising a future fix. Proponents say it is essential for industries where no alternative exists, like cement. The consensus is that CCS supplements but cannot replace emission reductions.
